position: both — mostly before a noun: *an alpha male*
contrast: Mostly heard in *alpha male* and *alpha female*. As a noun, *alpha* is the Greek letter and an early test version of software; in *an alpha release* that noun is only a modifier.

senses.gloss: Dominant and confident, acting as the leader of a group.
examples: He thinks he's the *alpha* male of the office.
The *alpha* wolf eats first.
She comes across as very *alpha* in meetings.

senses.gloss: Arranged in the order of the letters of the alphabet.
examples: Put the names in *alphabetical* order.
The guest list is *alphabetical* by last name.
There's an *alphabetical* index at the back of the book.

senses.gloss: Put in alphabetical order.
examples: She keeps an *alphabetized* list of every book she's read.
Are the files *alphabetized* by name or by date?
His spice rack is perfectly *alphabetized*.

senses.gloss: Made up of both letters and numbers.
examples: Your password must be at least eight *alphanumeric* characters.
Each package gets an *alphanumeric* tracking code.
The serial number is *alphanumeric*, so watch for the letter O versus zero.

contrast: Lowercase *alpine* describes any high mountains (*alpine lakes in Colorado*); capital *Alpine* means the Alps in Europe. *Alpine skiing* is downhill skiing.

senses.gloss: Found in or typical of high mountains.
examples: We hiked through *alpine* meadows full of wildflowers.
The lake sits in an *alpine* valley in the Rockies.
Few trees grow in the *alpine* zone above eleven thousand feet.

senses.gloss: Changed, so that it is different from what it was.
examples: The bank spotted an *altered* signature on the check.
Some drugs produce an *altered* state of consciousness.
Her whole manner seemed *altered* after the trip.

contrast: The adjective *alternate* is a different word: *on alternate days* means every other day, and *an alternate route* is a substitute one.

senses.gloss: Happening or arranged by turns, first one thing and then the other.
examples: The floor has *alternating* black and white tiles.
Outlets in the US supply *alternating* current.
The forecast calls for *alternating* rain and sun.

senses.gloss: Caring about other people's good more than your own.
examples: Her reasons for volunteering were purely *altruistic*.
It was an *altruistic* gesture, and he expected nothing back.
Some animals show surprisingly *altruistic* behavior.

contrast: Also a noun: *She's an amateur*. For the negative meaning, *amateurish* is more common in writing.

senses.gloss: Doing something for pleasure, not as a paid job.
examples: He's an *amateur* photographer with a real eye.
The *amateur* league plays on Saturday mornings.

senses.gloss: Done without skill; not looking professional.
examples: The website looks really *amateur*.
Their second video looked even *more amateur* than the first.

senses.gloss: Done badly, without the skill of a professional.
examples: The acting was painfully *amateurish*.
It was an *amateurish* mistake for someone with his experience.
The *most amateurish* part of the film was the sound.

contrast: Also a noun for the fossil resin itself. Americans call the middle traffic light *yellow*; *amber* there is British.

senses.gloss: Having the deep yellow-orange color of amber.
examples: The beer poured a clear *amber* color.
Her eyes looked almost *amber* in the sunlight.
*Amber* streetlights lined the old road.

senses.gloss: Able to use both hands equally well; of a tool, made for either hand.
examples: The pitcher is *ambidextrous* and can throw with either arm.
Only about one percent of people are truly *ambidextrous*.
The mouse has an *ambidextrous* design, so lefties can use it too.

senses.gloss: Present in the surrounding area.
examples: Store the medicine at *ambient* temperature.
The camera works well even in low *ambient* light.
*Ambient* noise from the highway makes it hard to sleep.

senses.gloss: Of music or sound: quiet and atmospheric, meant for the background.
examples: The spa plays soft *ambient* music all day.
He records *ambient* tracks for video games.

senses.gloss: Having more than one possible meaning; not clear.
examples: The wording of the contract is *ambiguous*.
She gave an *ambiguous* answer, and I still don't know if she's coming.
The ending of the movie is deliberately *ambiguous*.

contrast: Not *indifferent*: an *ambivalent* person has feelings both ways, not no feelings. *ambiguous* describes meaning, not feelings.

senses.gloss: Having mixed feelings about something, both positive and negative.
examples: I'm still *ambivalent* about moving to Denver.
Many voters feel *ambivalent* toward both candidates.
She has an *ambivalent* relationship with her hometown.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Of a patient: able to walk.
examples: The patient is *ambulatory* and can go home tomorrow.
*Ambulatory* residents eat in the main dining room.

senses.gloss: Of medical care: given to patients who do not stay overnight in the hospital.
examples: The clinic offers *ambulatory* surgery.
*Ambulatory* care centers are opening all over the suburbs.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *to*

senses.gloss: Willing to accept or agree to something.
examples: My boss is *amenable* to working from home on Fridays.
They seemed *amenable* to a lower price.

senses.gloss: Able to be treated or dealt with in a particular way.
examples: The condition is *amenable* to surgery.
Not every problem is *amenable* to a quick fix.

position: attributive only — in legal writing also *as amended* after the noun

senses.gloss: Officially changed to correct or improve it.
examples: You'll need to file an *amended* tax return.
The committee passed an *amended* version of the bill.
Please sign the *amended* contract and send it back.

contrast: *amiable* describes a person or their manner; *amicable* describes an agreement or relationship between people (*an amicable divorce*).

senses.gloss: Friendly and pleasant.
examples: Our new neighbor is an *amiable* guy who waves at everyone.
The meeting was surprisingly *amiable*.
He's much *more amiable* after his morning coffee.

contrast: *amicable* describes an agreement or relationship; *amiable* describes a person (*an amiable guy*).

senses.gloss: Friendly and without arguing, especially when settling a disagreement.
examples: The divorce was *amicable*, and they still co-parent well.
Both sides hope for an *amicable* agreement.
They parted on *amicable* terms.

position: predicative only — after *be* or *seem*, or right after *something*, *nothing*, *anything*
contrast: In *take something amiss* (обидеться) and *would not go amiss* (не помешает) it works as an adverb; both are fixed phrases.

senses.gloss: Wrong, or not as it should be.
examples: I knew something was *amiss* when I saw the front door open.
Nothing seemed *amiss* at first.
Did you notice anything *amiss* in the report?

senses.gloss: Showing or feeling romantic or sexual desire.
examples: He wrote her *amorous* letters from overseas.
The couple got a little too *amorous* on the dance floor.
She turned down his *amorous* advances.

senses.gloss: Having no clear shape, structure or definition.
examples: An *amorphous* gray blob showed up on the scan.
The plan is still pretty *amorphous*.
Wellness has become an *amorphous* term.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Able to live or move both on land and in water.
examples: Frogs are *amphibious* animals.
Tourists ride an *amphibious* bus that drives right into the river.

senses.gloss: Of a military operation: moving troops from the sea onto land.
examples: The Marines trained for an *amphibious* landing.
D-Day was the largest *amphibious* assault in history.

comparison: more/most — *more ample*, *most ample*; *ampler* and *amplest* are rare

senses.gloss: More than enough.
examples: There's *ample* parking behind the building.
You'll have *ample* time to finish the test.
The evidence was more than *ample*.

senses.gloss: Large and roomy; of a person's body, full and rounded.
examples: The minivan has *ample* room for five kids.
She had an *ample* figure and a big laugh.

senses.gloss: Building up muscle or other body tissue.
examples: He was banned for using *anabolic* steroids.
Protein triggers an *anabolic* response after exercise.
Some supplements claim *anabolic* effects they don't have.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a different period of time; out of date.
examples: A wristwatch in a movie about ancient Rome would be *anachronistic*.
The law is *anachronistic* and should be repealed.
Some find the tradition charming; others find it *anachronistic*.

position: both — sense 1 before a noun, sense 2 usually after a verb
contrast: Sense 2 is short for *anal retentive*; it is informal and a little rude, so keep it out of work emails.

senses.gloss: Relating to the anus.
examples: The doctor checked for an *anal* fissure.
Dogs sometimes need their *anal* glands cleaned.

senses.gloss: Informal: too worried about small details and neatness.
examples: He's really *anal* about how the dishwasher is loaded.
Don't be so *anal* — nobody will notice the typo.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *an anal-retentive boss*
contrast: Informal and a bit rude. The short form is *anal*.

senses.gloss: Too concerned with order, neatness and small details.
examples: My roommate is so *anal retentive* that she labels the shelves.
He's an *anal-retentive* editor who checks every comma.
I'll admit I'm a little *anal retentive* about my calendar.

contrast: Often a noun: *an analgesic* is a painkiller.

senses.gloss: Relieving pain.
examples: Aspirin has *analgesic* and anti-inflammatory effects.
The cream contains a mild *analgesic* ingredient.
Researchers are testing the plant's *analgesic* properties.

contrast: American spelling; *analogue* is British. The noun *analog* means a similar thing (*a meat analog*); the adjective meaning 'similar' is *analogous*.

senses.gloss: Not digital; showing information with hands, dials or continuous signals.
examples: I still wear an *analog* watch.
The old TV only picks up an *analog* signal.
Vinyl fans say *analog* sound is warmer.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *to*
contrast: Russian *аналогичный* is usually just *similar* in English; *analogous* is formal and points to a comparison of structure or function.

senses.gloss: Similar in some way, so that a comparison can be made.
examples: The situation is *analogous* to a patient refusing medicine.
The heart works in a way *analogous* to a pump.
Birds and bats have *analogous* wings.

position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Good at thinking carefully and logically about things.
examples: She has a very *analytical* mind.
He's the *most analytical* person on the team.

senses.gloss: Using or relating to analysis.
examples: The lab uses *analytical* chemistry to test the water.
The report takes an *analytical* approach to the data.

senses.gloss: Relating to a sudden, severe allergic reaction.
examples: A bee sting sent him into *anaphylactic* shock.
She carries an EpiPen in case of an *anaphylactic* reaction.
Peanuts can cause *anaphylactic* symptoms within minutes.

contrast: *anarchic* means chaotic or wildly unconventional; *anarchist* describes the political movement (*anarchist groups*).

senses.gloss: Without order or control; wild and chaotic.
examples: The first week of school was pretty *anarchic*.
The city felt *anarchic* after the storm knocked out power.
The show is known for its *anarchic* humor.

senses.gloss: Relating to the structure of the body.
examples: Leonardo made detailed *anatomical* drawings.
The model shows every *anatomical* detail of the heart.
There are small *anatomical* differences between the two species.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or inherited from your ancestors.
examples: They visited their *ancestral* village in Italy.
The family still owns its *ancestral* home in Virginia.
The tribe is fighting to protect its *ancestral* lands.

senses.gloss: Giving extra help or support; less important than the main thing.
examples: The hospital hired more *ancillary* staff.
Parking and meals are *ancillary* costs.
These duties are *ancillary* to your main job.

contrast: Also a noun: a person from Andalusia, or a breed of horse.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Andalusia, in southern Spain.
examples: We had *Andalusian* gazpacho in Seville.
The *Andalusian* coast is hot and dry in summer.
Flamenco is a big part of *Andalusian* culture.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the Andes mountains of South America.
examples: Quinoa is an ancient *Andean* crop.
They trekked through remote *Andean* villages.
Llamas are common in the *Andean* highlands.

senses.gloss: Not clearly male or female in appearance.
examples: The singer is known for an *androgynous* style.
Short hair made her look *more androgynous*.
The brand sells *androgynous* clothing for everyone.

contrast: Not funny: *anecdotal evidence* means people's stories, not scientific data. Russian *анекдотичный* (смешной, нелепый) is a false friend.

senses.gloss: Based on personal stories rather than careful research.
examples: The evidence for the diet is mostly *anecdotal*.
We have *anecdotal* reports of the problem, but no data yet.
His claims are purely *anecdotal*.

contrast: American spelling; British *anaemic*.

senses.gloss: Having too few red blood cells, so you feel weak and tired.
examples: She was *anemic* during her pregnancy.
*Anemic* patients often look pale.

senses.gloss: Weak, with little energy or growth.
examples: The economy showed *anemic* growth last quarter.
Sales were even *more anemic* than expected.

contrast: Usually a noun: *a local anesthetic*. British spelling *anaesthetic*. Don't mix it up with *aesthetic* (эстетический).

senses.gloss: Causing a loss of feeling or pain.
examples: The dentist rubbed an *anesthetic* gel on my gums.
The drug has a mild *anesthetic* effect.
Clove oil has natural *anesthetic* properties.

senses.gloss: Very beautiful, good or innocent, like an angel.
examples: The baby has an *angelic* face.
She sang the solo in an *angelic* voice.
The kids looked *angelic* — until the adults left the room.

contrast: In the US, the church in the Anglican family is called the *Episcopal* Church.

senses.gloss: Of the Church of England or the churches connected with it.
examples: He was raised in an *Anglican* family.
The *Anglican* bishops met in London.
The service followed the *Anglican* prayer book.

senses.gloss: Of the Germanic peoples who lived in England before 1066, or of their language.
examples: *Anglo-Saxon* kings ruled much of England.
Many short English words have *Anglo-Saxon* roots.

senses.gloss: Of English or northern European descent, especially white Protestant Americans.
examples: The town's founders were mostly *Anglo-Saxon* Protestants.
He changed his last name to something that sounded more *Anglo-Saxon*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Angola, in southern Africa.
examples: *Angolan* oil exports fell last year.
She's married to an *Angolan* musician.
The stew is traditionally *Angolan*.

senses.gloss: Showing or feeling great pain or worry.
examples: We heard an *anguished* cry from the next room.
The parents looked *anguished* as they waited for news.
She wrote an *anguished* letter to her son.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
comparison: more/most — in senses 1 and 2: *more angular*, *most angular*

senses.gloss: Having sharp corners or angles.
examples: The building has an *angular* modern design.
Her handwriting is tall and *angular*.
The new model is *more angular* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Of a person: thin, so that the bones show.
examples: He has an *angular* face with high cheekbones.
She was tall and *angular*, all elbows and knees.

senses.gloss: Technical: measured by an angle.
examples: Physics students learn about *angular* momentum.
The satellite's *angular* speed stays constant.

contrast: Usually a noun. In *animal fat* or *animal rights* it is a noun used as a modifier. The adjective means bodily and instinctive, as in Russian *животный страх*.

senses.gloss: Physical and instinctive, not controlled by thought.
examples: Fear is an *animal* instinct.
The actor had a kind of *animal* magnetism.
She felt a rush of *animal* panic in the dark.

senses.gloss: Like an animal; wild, physical or uncontrolled.
examples: The crowd's behavior turned *animalistic*.
The dancers moved with an *animalistic* energy.
His *animalistic* grunts at the gym annoy everyone.

position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Lively and full of energy or interest.
examples: They had an *animated* discussion about politics.
He gets *more animated* when he talks about baseball.

senses.gloss: Made from drawings, models or computer images that seem to move.
examples: Pixar makes *animated* movies.
The kids watch *animated* shows on Saturday mornings.

form: compound — noun + adjective: *ankle* + *deep*; same pattern as *knee-deep*, *waist-deep*
contrast: Also works as an adverb: *We waded ankle-deep into the creek*.

senses.gloss: Deep enough to reach your ankles.
examples: The water in the basement was *ankle-deep*.
We walked through *ankle-deep* mud to get to the barn.
By morning the snow was *ankle-deep*.

position: attributive only — after a verb say *held every year*
contrast: Also a noun: *an annual* is a plant that lives one year, or a book published once a year.

senses.gloss: Happening once every year.
examples: The company holds an *annual* picnic in July.
Don't forget your *annual* checkup.

senses.gloss: Calculated over a period of one year.
examples: Her *annual* salary is $85,000.
The town gets about forty inches of *annual* rainfall.

senses.gloss: Of a plant: living for only one year.
examples: Marigolds are *annual* flowers.
Plant *annual* herbs like basil after the last frost.

senses.gloss: Carefully inoffensive, and so bland and dull.
examples: The press release was full of *anodyne* corporate language.
Her speech was polite but *anodyne*.
He gave the *most anodyne* answer he could think of.

senses.gloss: Different from what is normal or expected.
examples: The test gave an *anomalous* result, so we ran it again.
A January that warm is *anomalous* for Chicago.
Scientists could not explain the *anomalous* readings.

comparison: not gradable — except in sense 2: *more anonymous*

senses.gloss: With a name that is not known or not made public.
examples: The money came from an *anonymous* donor.
The source asked to remain *anonymous*.
Police received an *anonymous* tip.

senses.gloss: Without any special features; impersonal.
examples: We stayed in an *anonymous* hotel near the airport.
Life in a big city can feel *anonymous*.

contrast: Also a noun (*an anorexic*), though many people prefer *a person with anorexia*. Calling a thin person *anorexic* as a joke is offensive.

senses.gloss: Having anorexia, an eating disorder in which a person refuses to eat enough.
examples: She was *anorexic* as a teenager.
The clinic treats *anorexic* patients.
Her doctor was worried she had become *anorexic*.

senses.gloss: Responsible for something and required to explain it to someone.
examples: The police chief is *answerable* to the mayor.
You'll be *answerable* for any damage to the car.
No one at the agency seemed *answerable* for the mistake.

senses.gloss: Showing opposition or hostility.
examples: He's always *antagonistic* toward reporters.
Their relationship became openly *antagonistic*.
The two drugs have *antagonistic* effects.

contrast: Many Americans drop the first *c* sound: ant-AHR-tik. *The Antarctic* is also a noun for the region; the continent is *Antarctica*.

senses.gloss: Of the region around the South Pole.
examples: Emperor penguins live in *Antarctic* waters.
Scientists spend the winter at an *Antarctic* research station.
*Antarctic* ice is melting faster than expected.

contrast: In American English it almost always means before the Civil War of 1861, especially in the South.

senses.gloss: From the period before the American Civil War.
examples: The tour includes three *antebellum* mansions.
*Antebellum* Southern society depended on slavery.
She teaches a course on *antebellum* literature.

senses.gloss: Relating to the study of human societies and cultures.
examples: She did *anthropological* fieldwork in Guatemala.
The museum has a large *anthropological* collection.
The book takes an *anthropological* look at office life.

senses.gloss: Having a human form or human qualities.
examples: Mickey Mouse is an *anthropomorphic* character.
Ancient peoples worshiped *anthropomorphic* gods.
The robot's design is almost *anthropomorphic*.

form: anti- + *American*; keep the hyphen and the capital

senses.gloss: Opposed to the United States, its policies or its people.
examples: Protesters chanted *anti-American* slogans.
The editorial was openly *anti-American*.
The mood in the region grew *more anti-American* after the war.

form: anti- + *intellectual*; the hyphen separates the two i's

senses.gloss: Hostile to education, experts or serious thinking.
examples: He criticized the *anti-intellectual* tone of the campaign.
The show is proudly *anti-intellectual*.
Some worry that public debate has become *more anti-intellectual*.

contrast: Also spelled *antisemitic*, which many style guides now prefer. Either way it means hostile to Jews only, not to all Semitic peoples.

senses.gloss: Hostile to or prejudiced against Jewish people.
examples: Someone painted *anti-Semitic* graffiti on the synagogue.
The comments were clearly *anti-Semitic*.
The group was condemned for its *anti-Semitic* views.

senses.gloss: Designed to shoot down enemy aircraft.
examples: *Antiaircraft* guns lined the harbor.
The plane was hit by *antiaircraft* fire.
The army moved *antiaircraft* missiles closer to the border.

senses.gloss: Killing bacteria or stopping them from growing.
examples: Wash your hands with *antibacterial* soap.
Honey has natural *antibacterial* properties.
Is this spray really *antibacterial*?

senses.gloss: Used or acting against cancer.
examples: The company is developing a new *anticancer* drug.
Broccoli may have *anticancer* benefits.
The trial compared three *anticancer* treatments.

senses.gloss: Happening or done because you expect something to happen.
examples: Therapists talk about *anticipatory* grief before a death.
The crowd let out an *anticipatory* cheer.
The central bank made an *anticipatory* rate cut.

contrast: Spelled *-climactic* (from *climax*), not ✗ *anticlimatic* (from *climate*).

senses.gloss: Disappointing because it is much less exciting than expected.
examples: After all the hype, the finale was *anticlimactic*.
The ending felt even *more anticlimactic* the second time.
It was an *anticlimactic* end to a great season.

senses.gloss: Killing fungus or stopping it from growing.
examples: The doctor prescribed an *antifungal* cream.
Tea tree oil is said to be *antifungal*.
Runners use *antifungal* powder in their shoes.

senses.gloss: Killing germs such as bacteria and fungi, or stopping them from growing.
examples: Hospitals use *antimicrobial* surfaces in operating rooms.
The fabric is treated to be *antimicrobial*.
Overuse of *antimicrobial* drugs creates resistant germs.

senses.gloss: Designed to kill or injure people rather than destroy vehicles or buildings.
examples: Many countries have banned *antipersonnel* mines.
The bomb scattered *antipersonnel* fragments.
The treaty covers *antipersonnel* weapons only.

contrast: Also a noun: *an antiquarian* collects or sells old things.

senses.gloss: Relating to collecting or selling old and rare things, especially books.
examples: He runs an *antiquarian* bookstore in Boston.
The fair attracts *antiquarian* dealers from all over the country.
She has an *antiquarian* interest in old maps.

contrast: *antiquated* is negative (too old to be useful); *antique* is neutral or positive (old and valuable).

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned and no longer suitable or useful.
examples: The office still runs on *antiquated* computers.
Some of these state laws are *antiquated*.
Their billing system is even *more antiquated* than ours.

contrast: Russian *античный* (Greek or Roman) is *ancient* or *classical* in English; *antique* means old and valuable, usually over a hundred years old. Also a noun: *She collects antiques*.

senses.gloss: Old and valuable, usually made a hundred or more years ago.
examples: We bought an *antique* dresser at an estate sale.
The *antique* clock still keeps perfect time.
Is that ring really *antique*?

contrast: Also spelled *anti-Semitic*. Many style guides, including AP, now prefer the closed spelling, since there is no 'Semitism' that the word opposes.

senses.gloss: Hostile to or prejudiced against Jewish people.
examples: The university condemned the *antisemitic* posters.
Reports of *antisemitic* incidents rose last year.
His remarks were widely seen as *antisemitic*.

contrast: Also a noun: *an antiseptic* is a substance that kills germs.

senses.gloss: Preventing infection by killing germs.
examples: Clean the cut with an *antiseptic* wipe.
The mouthwash has an *antiseptic* effect.

senses.gloss: So clean and plain that it feels cold and has no character.
examples: The new apartment felt *antiseptic* and unlived-in.
The hotel lobby was even *more antiseptic* than a hospital.

contrast: In everyday American English *antisocial* usually just means unsociable (*I'm feeling antisocial tonight*). In law and psychology it means harmful to others.

senses.gloss: Not wanting to spend time with other people.
examples: I'm feeling kind of *antisocial* tonight, so I'm staying in.
My brother gets *more antisocial* every year.

senses.gloss: Harmful to other people or to society.
examples: Vandalism is a form of *antisocial* behavior.
He was diagnosed with *antisocial* personality disorder.

senses.gloss: Designed to destroy or stop tanks.
examples: The soldiers carried *antitank* missiles.
The road was blocked with *antitank* barriers.
An *antitank* mine destroyed the truck.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *to*

senses.gloss: Directly opposed to or completely unlike something.
examples: Censorship is *antithetical* to a free press.
His views are *antithetical* to everything the party stands for.
They hold *antithetical* ideas about raising kids.

form: anti- + *trust*, an old word for a monopoly
contrast: An American term; British English usually says *competition law*.

senses.gloss: Designed to prevent monopolies and protect competition.
examples: The government filed an *antitrust* lawsuit against the company.
*Antitrust* regulators blocked the merger.
She's a lawyer who specializes in *antitrust* cases.

senses.gloss: Acting against viruses.
examples: Doctors may prescribe an *antiviral* drug for the flu.
She took *antiviral* medication for her shingles.
The compound turned out to be strongly *antiviral*.

form: -y from *ants*, as in *ants in your pants*
contrast: Informal and American.

senses.gloss: Restless and impatient, unable to sit still.
examples: The kids get *antsy* on long car rides.
I start feeling *antsy* if I stay home all weekend.
The longer the meeting went, the *antsier* everyone got.

senses.gloss: Not interested and not caring; unwilling to make an effort.
examples: Young voters are often called *apathetic*.
He's totally *apathetic* about his grades.
The crowd gave an *apathetic* round of applause.

senses.gloss: Describing or looking like the total destruction of the world.
examples: The movie shows an *apocalyptic* future after a nuclear war.
After the wildfire, the town looked *apocalyptic*.
Some of the climate warnings sound almost *apocalyptic*.

contrast: Russian *апокрифический* is mostly about religious texts; in everyday English *apocryphal* means a story is famous but probably not true.

senses.gloss: Widely told but probably not true.
examples: The story about George Washington and the cherry tree is *apocryphal*.
There's an *apocryphal* tale that Einstein failed math.
Most of those celebrity quotes online are *apocryphal*.

senses.gloss: Not interested in politics, or not connected with it.
examples: My parents were totally *apolitical*.
The organization tries to stay *apolitical*.
It was supposed to be an *apolitical* event, but people argued anyway.

senses.gloss: Showing or saying that you are sorry.
examples: The manager was very *apologetic* about the mix-up.
She gave me an *apologetic* smile.
He sounded *apologetic* for calling so late.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry.
examples: My dad was *apoplectic* when he saw the phone bill.
Fans were *apoplectic* over the referee's call.
She was practically *apoplectic* with rage.

contrast: Many people from the region say ap-uh-LATCH-uhn and hear LAY as an outsider's pronunciation.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the Appalachian Mountains or the region around them in the eastern US.
examples: They hiked part of the *Appalachian* Trail.
Her grandparents grew up in an *Appalachian* coal town.
Bluegrass has deep *Appalachian* roots.

form: -ed — how you feel; from the verb *appall*
contrast: *appalled* is how you feel; *appalling* is what causes the feeling. The American spelling of the verb is *appall*.

senses.gloss: Shocked and upset by something very bad.
examples: I was *appalled* at the condition of the kitchen.
She gave him an *appalled* look.
We were *appalled* to learn that nobody had called for help.

form: -ing — what causes the feeling; from the verb *appall*
contrast: *appalling* is what causes the feeling; *appalled* is how you feel.

senses.gloss: Shocking and morally very bad.
examples: The prisoners lived in *appalling* conditions.
It's *appalling* that children are going hungry.

senses.gloss: Informal: very bad in quality.
examples: The service at that restaurant was *appalling*.
His spelling is even *more appalling* than mine.

contrast: Nothing to do with a court appeal: Russian *апелляционный* is *appellate*. *appeal to* means attract: *The idea appeals to me*.

senses.gloss: Attractive or interesting.
examples: The job offer is very *appealing*.
Lower prices make the plan *more appealing* to families.
She has an *appealing* smile.

senses.gloss: Relating to appeals, in which a higher court reviews a lower court's decision.
examples: The case went to an *appellate* court.
She's an *appellate* lawyer in Washington.
The *appellate* judges overturned the conviction.

senses.gloss: Looking or smelling good enough to make you want to eat.
examples: The dishes in the menu photos look very *appetizing*.
An *appetizing* smell came from the kitchen.
Cold, soggy fries aren't very *appetizing*.

contrast: Also stressed uh-PLIK-uh-buhl. On forms, *N/A* stands for *not applicable*.

senses.gloss: Relevant to or affecting a particular person or situation.
examples: The rules are *applicable* to all employees.
Fill in your middle name, if *applicable*.
Contractors must follow all *applicable* safety laws.
